title: Slide 1 · Sequence Modeling, Attention, and Transformers
question: If both occurrences of red use the same embedding, which number in that embedding tells us which red came first?
answer: Neither occurrence carries its position in the shared color embedding. We must preserve the row order and give the model some way to use it.

title: Slide 2 · Keep an ordered row for each occurrence
question: If a fourth signal is blue, which dimension changes?
answer: The number of positions grows from three to four. Each color still has two coordinates, so the shape becomes 4 × 2.

title: Slide 3 · Ask one question of all rows
question: What changes if the query becomes [0, 1]?
answer: The scores become [0, 1, 0]. This query picks out the blue coordinate, which is largest in the middle row.

title: Slide 4 · Turn scores into shares
question: Three equal scores enter the softmax. How much weight does each get?
answer: Their exponentials are identical. Each receives one third of their total, even if all three original scores are negative.

title: Slide 5 · Collect the values
question: If all three brightness values are 4, what comes out?
answer: The output is 4. Multiplying any shares that sum to one by the same value gives that value.

title: Slide 6 · Compute every query at once
question: Which row and column give the weight from the middle query to the final red?
answer: Use the second row and third column, A[1, 2] in Python. Rows ask the questions and columns identify the candidate keys.

title: Slide 7 · Give order a numerical representation
question: Does adding position information force the newest token to receive the most weight?
answer: No. This example chose offsets and a positive query that favor later positions. Learned projections can use or ignore those coordinates.

title: Slide 8 · Hide future positions
question: Can the second position see its own token during next-token training?
answer: Yes. It uses tokens one and two to predict token three. It would leak the answer if it could see token three.

title: Slide 9 · Build a trainable attention head
question: What makes this single-head layer self-attention?
answer: The same input sequence supplies every query, key and value. Each position draws information from positions in that sequence.

title: Slide 10 · Assemble a transformer block
question: If attention acts across positions, which part of this block can transform each position separately?
answer: The feedforward network uses the same learned transformation on each row. Its input already contains information mixed across positions by attention. The two runs also test information flow. With the causal mask, changing position three leaves the first two outputs unchanged.

title: Slide 12 · From this module to the next
question: A vocabulary contains four symbols. What must we compute from the final context vector before predicting the next symbol?
answer: Produce four scores, one per symbol, then normalize them into a probability distribution. That distribution lets us score the symbol that actually follows.

title: Office hours · Why do we need values when we already have keys?
question: Why do we need values when we already have keys?
answer: An item can match a question by color and contribute information about brightness. Separate projections let the model learn which coordinates determine a match and which coordinates to send once matched.

title: Office hours · Why do we need both position information and a mask?
question: Why do we need both position information and a mask?
answer: Position information gives the model a way to distinguish locations. A causal mask enforces a visibility rule. A position vector alone would still let a next-token predictor read a later token.

title: Office hours · Does a high attention weight explain the entire prediction?
question: Does a high attention weight explain the entire prediction?
answer: It describes one mixture at one head and layer. The size and direction of the value vector, other heads, later layers and residual paths also affect the prediction.

title: Exercise 1
question: A one-coordinate query is 1 and two keys are 0 and ln(3). Calculate the attention shares.
answer: The exponentials are 1 and 3. Their sum is 4, so the shares are 1/4 and 3/4.

title: Exercise 2
question: Use shares 1/4 and 3/4 with value vectors [4, 0] and [0, 8]. Compute the output.
answer: The coordinates are (1/4)4 + (3/4)0 = 1 and (1/4)0 + (3/4)8 = 6. The output is [1, 6].

title: Exercise 3
question: All scores are zero in a four-token stream. What is the third row of causal attention?
answer: Three keys are allowed and tie. Row three is [1/3, 1/3, 1/3, 0].

title: Exercise 4
question: A sequence has five positions, queries and keys have width two, and values have width three. Give the score and output shapes.
answer: Each of five queries compares with five keys, so the score shape is 5 × 5. Each query produces three output coordinates, giving 5 × 3.

title: Exercise 5
question: A fixed query attends to two tokens with no positions or mask. Swap their keys and values together. Explain the result.
answer: The two scores swap, their softmax weights swap and the same two weighted values are added in reverse order. The mixture is unchanged. A position-dependent key or a causal mask can break this symmetry.

title: Exercise 6
question: A student multiplies probabilities by a causal mask after softmax and gets an allowed row sum of 0.6. Repair the calculation.
answer: Mask the future scores before softmax. The denominator then sums only the permitted exponentials and the allowed weights sum to one.

title: Exercise 7
question: Change the first token of a three-token sequence and compare the last output of a causal block before and after. Must the last output change? May it change?
answer: It may change. The last position may read the first position. A change is not guaranteed, since the first token’s value might contribute little or its change might disappear in later layers.
